notes:
I've written notes for most verses of Habakkuk 2, but some sources are missing. I ran out of searches before I could read enduringword.com (Guzik), preceptaustin.org, netbible.org notes, or any Catholic, Orthodox or Wesley's own pages. I found no sources on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings, so that category is left out. Verses 6, 9, 12 and 19 have no separate notes; I only have overviews or grouped comments for them. Most notes come from Ellicott, Gill and other older commentators on biblehub.com and studylight.org.

## Habakkuk 2: Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- **Ellicott:** The picture is a watchman climbing high to see far (compare 2 Kings 9:17). He reads the last line as Habakkuk asking what answer God will give, through him, to his complaint. https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/2-1.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Gill (Baptist):** The prophet withdrew from the world to pray and meditate, and waited for God's answer. Gill says "reproved" could mean three things: rebuked by God for arguing so boldly, troubled by his own doubts about God's providence, or challenged by his people's objections. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/2-1.html
- **Geneva Study Bible (Reformed):** Habakkuk sets aside his own judgment and depends only on God for what to answer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/2-1.htm

**v. 2**
- **Ellicott:** "The tables" probably means known public tablets where prophets posted their messages. Calvin thought they hung in the Temple; Luther and Ewald thought in the marketplace. "Run" means the reader can take it in at a glance. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** It was written in large letters so a passer-by could read it in one look. It was written for the whole Church, not for Habakkuk himself. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/2-2.html
- **Kelly:** Kelly argues against the common view. The text doesn't say the runner may read; it says the reader may run and spread the good news. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/2-2.html
- **Gill:** Gill takes the vision as being about the Messiah's coming and the fall of the Church's enemies. It was written down so it could be read again and again in later times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/2-2.htm
- **Coffman (Restoration Movement, Arminian):** It was written so it would stay available to bless all later generations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/2-2.html
- **Keil–Delitzsch (scholarly):** They reject the public-noticeboard idea. "The tables" just means the tablets Habakkuk would write on. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/2-2.htm
- **Seedbed (Wesleyan):** The article on this chapter has a section titled "Write the Vision!" Its point is that the "proud" will not see the promise, but the righteous will claim it by faith. https://seedbed.com/the-just-shall-live-by-faith-in-what/

**v. 3**
- **Ellicott:** The vision "pants for the end," as if it longs to be fulfilled. He says the KJV's "it will not tarry" is a poor translation, since the prophet has just said it will tarry. The sense is that it won't be late for its appointed day. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Another commentator (not named on the page):** God's purpose moves on even when it seems slow to us. It cannot be hurried and does not linger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/habakkuk/2-3.htm
- **Gill:** Gill reads the last clause as "he that is coming will come," meaning the Messiah. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/habakkuk/2.htm

**v. 4: the verse where traditions differ most**
- **Ellicott (traditional reading):** The Babylonian is puffed up, and his pride pushes out every thought of God. The prophet leaves "so he will die" unsaid and jumps to the contrast. The promised "life" is rescue from destruction. Ellicott says we can't tell whether it also means life after death. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Ellicott on doctrine:** Whatever Paul did with the verse, in Habakkuk itself it carries no doctrinal meaning, though it matters a great deal for how we live. https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/2-4.htm
- **The opposite view on the same page:** Another note says the promise reaches to eternal reward, and that Paul's use of it for justification by faith in Christ follows naturally. https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/2-4.htm
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** Gill applies the verse to Christ. The proud man is the self-righteous Pharisee who trusts his own goodness. The "just" man trusts Christ's righteousness counted to him, not his own. Gill adds that faith itself is not what makes a person righteous. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/habakkuk/2.htm
- **"Faith" or "faithfulness"?** Some translations say faithfulness: Young's has "stedfastness" and the NET has "faithfulness." Kingsley's sermon says the oracle really means the righteous man lives "by his fidelity." https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/2-4.htm https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/wbt/habakkuk/2-4.html https://biblehub.com/sermons/habakkuk/2-4.htm
- **Lutheran (1517.org):** Luther came to see God's righteousness in Romans 1:17 as a pure gift. The article calls Habakkuk 2:4 the "litmus test" for how you understand the gospel. It says the only way through God's judgment is to hold fast to God's Word. https://www.1517.org/articles/faith-remains-from-habbakuk-to-luther
- **Luther's own comment:** In his Minor Prophets commentary, Luther says the righteous live by faith while they wait for the Lord. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/interpreting-faith-in-the-reformation-catholic-and-protestant-interpretations-of-habakkuk-24b-and-its-new-testament-quotations/
- **Reformed (TGC / Themelios article):** The article argues that Luther and Calvin made Christ and his work the object of the faith in 2:4b. It says Catholic writers pointed instead to the believer's faithful actions, and that the Council of Trent concluded both Christ's work and the sacraments are needed. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/interpreting-faith-in-the-reformation-catholic-and-protestant-interpretations-of-habakkuk-24b-and-its-new-testament-quotations/
  - Note: this is a Protestant article describing the Catholic view. I couldn't check it against Catholic sources.
- **Baptist (Piper, desiringgod.org):** The verse implies that righteous people are people of faith, and that faith is what saves from God's wrath and keeps them safe forever. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/the-just-shall-live-by-faith
- **Wesleyan (Seedbed):** Luther was right that justification is by faith in Christ. But the full meaning in Habakkuk is wider: living and acting now by faith in all of God's kingdom promises. https://seedbed.com/the-just-shall-live-by-faith-in-what/

**v. 5**
- **Ellicott:** He prefers the reading "wine is treacherous." On this reading the Babylonians are charged with drunkenness and greed as well as pride. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Gill:** Gill applies verses 5–8 to the Roman emperors, such as Nero and Domitian taking divine titles. This is a historicist reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/habakkuk-2.html

**vv. 6–8**
- **Ellicott:** Until now Babylon's downfall was only hinted at. Here it is announced in a taunt song put in the mouths of its victims. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Expositor's Bible:** Babylon is like a debtor piling up creditors who will one day collect every penny. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Gill on v. 8:** Gill takes "the remnant" as the Christians who survived the persecutions and rose to power under Constantine. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/habakkuk-2.html

**vv. 9–11**
- **Ellicott:** This is a woe on Babylon storing up plunder in a fortress it thinks can't be taken. Each stone in walls built by forced captive labour cries out against it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Ellicott on v. 10:** Babylon was piling up guilt on its own soul the whole time it plundered. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm

**vv. 12–13**
- **Ellicott:** The nations labour "only for the fire," as in Jeremiah 51:58. The slaves built Babylon's palaces only for fire to destroy them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm

**v. 14**
- **Ellicott:** The same promise appears in Isaiah 11:9. It is set against Babylon's short-lived glory. https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/2-14.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** God's glory would be seen in Babylon's overthrow. https://biblehub.com/habakkuk/2-14.htm

**vv. 15–16**
- **Ellicott:** The verses may describe drunken outrages by Babylonian soldiers. Ellicott prefers a figurative reading: Babylon made its neighbours drink the cup of its cruel anger. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Expositor's Bible:** The "cup of the LORD's right hand" is an old figure of speech that survived. It notes the taunts mostly stress that injustice tends to decay from within. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/habakkuk/2.htm

**v. 17**
- **Ellicott:** He probably has in view Babylon cutting Lebanon's cedars for its palaces. Others take "Lebanon" to stand for the Holy Land or the Temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm

**v. 18**
- **Ellicott:** The "teacher of lies" is the idol itself, not a false prophet. The Hebrew uses a play on words, something like "dumb nothings." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Gill:** Gill applies the verse to the images used in Roman Catholic worship. This is a Protestant polemical reading. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/habakkuk-2.html

**v. 20**
- **Ellicott:** While false worship carries on, the true ruler is in his temple. The prophet stops denouncing and turns to the hymn in chapter 3. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/habakkuk/2.htm
- **Gill:** Gill sees the verse as partly fulfilled on pagan Rome and on papal Rome at the Reformation, with complete fulfilment still to come. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/habakkuk/2-20.html
